segments.title: Your AI Pair Programmer
segments.content:
Coding with an AI Partner

AI pair programming transforms how you write, read, and maintain code. Your Avatar understands your codebase, follows your style, and catches bugs before they ship.

What an AI Pair Programmer Can Do

  1. Autocomplete on steroids: Suggests entire functions, not just the next line. Understands context from imports, comments, and surrounding code.
  2. Code generation: Turn a description into working code. Example: "Write a Python function that validates UK postcodes using regex."
  3. Explanation: Highlight any code and ask: "What does this do?" Get a plain-English breakdown with edge cases.
  4. Refactoring: "Make this function more readable" or "Convert this to async/await." The Avatar preserves logic while improving structure.
  5. Test generation: Automatically writes unit tests covering happy paths, edge cases, and error conditions.

Case Study: The Startup That Shipped 3x Faster

CodeBase, a 6-person dev team, integrated Zetrix into their VS Code workflow. Results after 3 months:

  • Boilerplate reduction: 40% less time writing repetitive setup code.
  • Bug catch rate: AI review caught 35% of bugs before human review.
  • Onboarding speed: New developers understood the codebase 50% faster using AI explanations.
  • Test coverage: From 45% to 82% with AI-generated tests.

Release cadence: from bi-weekly to twice weekly.

Step-by-Step: Setting Up Your Coding Environment

  1. Install the Zetrix IDE extension for VS Code, JetBrains, or Vim.
  2. Connect your code repository (GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket) in Integrations.
  3. Index your codebase. The Avatar scans files, learns your patterns, and builds a semantic map.
  4. Set your coding style preferences: language conventions, naming patterns (camelCase vs snake_case), max line length, and docstring format.
  5. Test with a real task. Open a file, write a comment describing a new function, and press Tab. Watch the Avatar generate the implementation.

Framework: The Pair Programming Protocol

When working with your AI partner, follow this protocol:

  • P – Plan: Describe what you want before asking for code.
  • A – Analyse: Review the generated code for correctness and security.
  • I – Iterate: Refine with specific feedback, not vague requests.
  • R – Run: Always test AI-generated code before committing.

Mindset Shift: You are the pilot. The Avatar is the copilot. You make architectural decisions; it handles syntax and boilerplate.

segments.title: Prompt Engineering for Code
segments.content:
Writing Prompts That Produce Great Code

Garbage in, garbage out. The quality of your code depends on the quality of your prompts. Master these patterns.

The CODE Prompt Framework

  1. C – Context: Provide the file path, language, and relevant imports. "In my utils.py file, which imports re and datetime..."
  2. O – Objective: Be specific. "Write a function that sanitises user input to prevent XSS attacks."
  3. D – Details: Specify inputs, outputs, and constraints. "Accept a string. Return a safe string. Do not use external libraries."
  4. E – Examples: Show expected input/output pairs. This reduces ambiguity dramatically.

Case Study: The 10-Minute vs. 2-Hour Feature

Developer A needed a function to parse CSV headers. Their prompt: "Parse CSV." Result: Generic code that did not handle edge cases. Time spent fixing: 2 hours.

Developer B used the CODE framework:

  • C: "In data_parser.py, Python 3.11, using only stdlib."
  • O: "Write a function that reads CSV headers and validates they match an expected schema."
  • D: "Return a dict mapping expected columns to found columns. Raise ValueError if any expected column is missing. Handle BOM and UTF-8 encoding."
  • E: Input: expected=["name","age"], file="users.csv". Output: {"name": "name", "age": "age"} or raises ValueError.

Result: Working code in 10 minutes. Zero fixes needed.

Step-by-Step: Crafting a Perfect Code Prompt

  1. Identify the task. Example: "Sort a list of employees by start date, then by last name."
  2. Add context: "In my HR module (hr/sorting.py), using Python 3.11. Employee objects have .start_date (datetime) and .last_name (str)."
  3. Define constraints: "Do not mutate the original list. Handle None start_dates by placing them last."
  4. Provide examples: 
    Input: [Alice(2023-01-15), Bob(None), Charlie(2022-06-01)]
Output: [Charlie, Alice, Bob]
  5. Ask for tests: "Include unit tests using pytest."
  6. Review the output. If wrong, do not rewrite the whole prompt. Isolate the error: "The None handling is reversed. Place Nones last, not first."

Anti-Patterns to Avoid

  • Vague prompts: "Fix this" → "Fix the off-by-one error in the loop on line 42."
  • Too much context: Including 500 lines of unrelated code confuses the model.
  • No examples: The Avatar guesses your intent. Examples make it certain.
  • Asking for everything at once: Break large tasks into 2–3 smaller prompts.

Framework: The Prompt Refinement Loop

When output is wrong, diagnose before rewriting:

  1. Identify the specific error: What exactly is wrong?
  2. Check context: Did you provide enough file/function context?
  3. Add an example: One input/output pair often fixes ambiguity.
  4. Constrain: Add a "Do not..." or "Always..." rule.
  5. Re-test: Verify the fix before moving on.

segments.title: Debugging with AI
segments.content:
Finding and Fixing Bugs Faster

Debugging is detective work. Your Avatar is Sherlock Holmes with infinite patience and perfect memory.

Step-by-Step: AI-Powered Debugging

  1. Describe the symptom: "When I submit the form, the page hangs for 30 seconds then shows a 500 error."
  2. Share the error: Paste the stack trace, log output, or screenshot. The Avatar traces the error to its root cause.
  3. Provide context: Share the relevant file(s), recent changes, and environment (OS, language version, framework).
  4. Ask for hypotheses: "What are the 3 most likely causes?" The Avatar ranks them by probability.
  5. Test each hypothesis: The Avatar suggests diagnostic code or logging to narrow down the cause.
  6. Apply the fix: Once identified, the Avatar suggests a patch. Review it carefully before applying.
  7. Prevent recurrence: Ask the Avatar to write a regression test and update documentation.

Case Study: The Production Outage That Lasted 12 Minutes

ShopFast's checkout page went down at 14:00 on Black Friday. Their lead developer used AI debugging:

  • Symptom: 500 errors on /checkout, affecting 15% of users.
  • Error: "ConnectionTimeout: Redis at redis-prod:6379"
  • Context: Recent deploy added session caching. Redis cluster has 3 nodes.
  • Hypotheses: 1) Redis node failure, 2) Connection pool exhaustion, 3) Network partition.
  • Diagnostic: Avatar suggested checking connection pool size and Redis node health.
  • Root cause: Connection pool defaulted to 10. Black Friday traffic needed 100+.
  • Fix: Increase pool size, add connection retry logic. Deployed in 8 minutes.

Total downtime: 12 minutes. Estimated revenue saved: £2M.

Advanced Debugging Techniques

  • Diff debugging: "This worked yesterday. Here is the diff since then. What broke?" The Avatar highlights risky changes.
  • Log analysis: Paste 1,000 lines of logs. The Avatar summarises patterns, anomalies, and timelines.
  • Performance profiling: Share a CPU or memory profile. The Avatar identifies bottlenecks and suggests optimisations.
  • Replay debugging: Describe the exact sequence of actions. The Avatar reconstructs the state at each step.

Framework: The DEBUG Protocol

Follow this structured approach for every bug:

  • D – Detect: What is the symptom? Who reported it? When did it start?
  • E – Examine: Collect logs, stack traces, and reproduction steps.
  • B – Build hypotheses: What are the 3 most likely causes?
  • U – Test hypotheses: Add logging, isolate variables, reproduce locally.
  • G – Generate fix: Apply the smallest possible patch.

Golden Rule: Never blindly apply AI-suggested fixes. Always understand the root cause before patching.

segments.title: AI Code Review
segments.content:
Catching Issues Before They Reach Production

Code review is essential but time-consuming. Your Avatar performs first-pass reviews in seconds, freeing human reviewers for architecture and design.

Step-by-Step: Automated Code Review

  1. Create a Code Review Agent in Agent Studio.
  2. Upload your style guide and security checklist to PKM. Example files: "Python-Style-Guide.md" and "Security-Checklist.md."
  3. Write the system prompt:
    "You are a senior engineer. Review the provided code for: correctness, readability, performance, security, and test coverage. Reference specific lines. Suggest improvements, not just criticisms."
  4. Configure triggers:
    • On pull request creation.
    • On commit to develop branch.
    • Manual trigger for ad-hoc reviews.
  5. The agent produces a review report:
    • Summary score (1–10).
    • Critical issues (must fix).
    • Warnings (should fix).
    • Suggestions (nice to have).
    • Positive highlights (what was done well).
  6. Human reviewers focus on the critical issues and architectural feedback. The Avatar handled the typos, style violations, and obvious bugs.

Case Study: The Team That Halved Review Time

DevTeamX had a 48-hour code review SLA. Reviews were thorough but slow, blocking releases. After adding an AI first-pass:

  • AI review time: 30 seconds per PR.
  • Human review time: Reduced from 2 hours to 45 minutes per PR.
  • Bugs caught pre-merge: +40% (Avatar never misses an off-by-one error).
  • Developer satisfaction: Up 25% (faster feedback = happier team).

What the Avatar Reviews

  • Syntax errors and type mismatches.
  • Security vulnerabilities: SQL injection, XSS, insecure dependencies.
  • Performance issues: N+1 queries, unbounded loops, memory leaks.
  • Style consistency: naming, formatting, docstrings.
  • Test coverage: untested branches, missing edge cases.

Framework: The Review Severity Matrix

Classify every finding:

  • Critical: Security risk, data loss, crash. Must fix before merge.
  • Warning: Performance concern, unclear logic. Should fix before merge.
  • Suggestion: Style improvement, optimisation. Nice to have.
  • Praise: Well-designed pattern, good test coverage. Reinforce excellence.

segments.title: API Building with AI
segments.content:
From Specification to Endpoint

Building APIs is repetitive but critical. Your Avatar generates endpoints, documentation, and tests from a simple description.

Step-by-Step: API Development Workflow

  1. Write an OpenAPI specification or a plain-English description. Example: "I need a REST API for a task manager. Endpoints: GET /tasks, POST /tasks, GET /tasks/{id}, PUT /tasks/{id}, DELETE /tasks/{id}."
  2. Prompt the Avatar: "Generate a FastAPI implementation with SQLAlchemy models, Pydantic schemas, and CRUD operations."
  3. The Avatar produces:
    • main.py with route definitions.
    • models.py with database schemas.
    • schemas.py with request/response validation.
    • crud.py with database operations.
    • database.py with connection handling.
  4. Review the generated code. Check for SQL injection risks, missing auth, and incorrect HTTP status codes.
  5. Prompt for documentation: "Generate Swagger UI annotations and a README with curl examples."
  6. Prompt for tests: "Write pytest tests for all endpoints, including 404 and 422 cases."
  7. Run the tests. Fix any failures. The Avatar helps debug test issues.

Case Study: The MVP in 48 Hours

Solo founder Priya needed an API for her fitness tracking app. Traditional estimate: 2 weeks. With her Avatar:

  • Hour 1: Described the API in plain English.
  • Hour 2: Avatar generated FastAPI scaffold with auth and DB models.
  • Hour 6: Added 8 endpoints. Avatar wrote tests. 94% passing.
  • Hour 12: Avatar generated Swagger docs and README.
  • Hour 24: Deployed to AWS. Shared with beta testers.
  • Hour 48: First paying customer signed up.

Time to market: 48 hours instead of 2 weeks. Cost: $0 (her time only).

Advanced: GraphQL and gRPC

  • GraphQL: Describe your data model. The Avatar generates schema, resolvers, and dataloaders for N+1 protection.
  • gRPC: Write a .proto file. The Avatar generates server stubs, client code, and interceptors.

Framework: The API Quality Checklist

Before deploying any API:

  • Validation: Are all inputs validated? (Pydantic, Joi, etc.)
  • Auth: Are protected endpoints actually protected?
  • Errors: Do error responses include helpful messages and correct status codes?
  • Tests: Is every endpoint tested for success AND failure cases?
  • Docs: Is there auto-generated documentation (Swagger, Redoc)?
  • Rate limiting: Are brute-force attacks prevented?

segments.title: No-Code & Low-Code Development
segments.content:
Building Without Writing Code

Not every problem needs a custom application. No-code tools let you build fast, iterate faster, and involve non-technical team members.

Step-by-Step: No-Code App Creation

  1. Define the problem. Example: "We need an internal tool to track employee vacation requests."
  2. Choose a platform:
    • Notion / Airtable: Database + views + forms. Best for simple workflows.
    • Webflow / Framer: Design-driven websites with CMS. Best for marketing sites.
    • Bubble / Adalo: Full web apps with logic, auth, and payments. Best for MVPs.
    • Zapier / Make: Automation between tools. Best for connecting existing systems.
  3. Design the data model. What entities exist? What are their properties and relationships?
  4. Prompt your Avatar: "Convert this data model into an Airtable base schema with linked tables and formula fields."
  5. Build the UI. Use the platform's drag-and-drop editor. The Avatar suggests layouts and UX patterns.
  6. Add logic. Example: "When status changes to Approved, send an email to HR and update the calendar." The Avatar writes the automation rules.
  7. Test with 3 real users. Collect feedback. Iterate in hours, not weeks.

Case Study: The HR Tool Built in a Day

HR manager Lisa needed a vacation request system. IT quoted 3 months and £15,000. She built it in Airtable with Avatar help:

  • Data model: Employees, Requests, Balances, Approvers.
  • Form: Employees submit via Airtable form.
  • Logic: Auto-calculate remaining balance. Route to manager. Notify HR on approval.
  • Dashboard: Calendar view of team availability.

Build time: 6 hours. Cost: $20/month. IT involvement: zero.

When to Use No-Code vs Code

  • No-Code: Internal tools, MVPs, prototypes, event registration, simple CRUD apps.
  • Low-Code: Apps needing custom logic but standard UI. Example: Retool dashboards.
  • Code: High-scale systems, unique algorithms, strict compliance, performance-critical paths.

Framework: The Build vs. Buy Decision Matrix

Before building anything, score each option 1–10:

  • Speed: How fast can we deploy?
  • Cost: What's the total cost of ownership?
  • Customisation: How unique are our needs?
  • Scale: Will this need to handle 10x growth?
  • Maintenance: Who will maintain it long-term?

If no-code wins on 3+ dimensions, build with no-code. If code wins, write code.

segments.title: Git & Documentation
segments.content:
Version Control and Knowledge Sharing

Code lives in Git. Knowledge lives in docs. Your Avatar helps with both, ensuring your team moves fast without breaking things.

Step-by-Step: Git Workflow with AI

  1. Branch naming: Prompt: "Suggest a branch name for adding OAuth2 login." Output: "feature/oauth2-login"
  2. Commit messages: Stage your changes. Prompt: "Write a conventional commit message for these changes." The Avatar follows the conventional commits spec.
  3. PR descriptions: Paste the branch diff. The Avatar generates a structured PR description with summary, changes, testing notes, and screenshots placeholder.
  4. Merge conflict resolution: Paste the conflict markers. The Avatar explains both versions and suggests a resolution.
  5. Release notes: Provide a list of merged PRs. The Avatar categorises into Features, Fixes, Breaking Changes, and Deprecations.

Case Study: The Team That Stopped Writing Bad Commits

Team Alpha had 50+ developers. Commit messages were a mess: "fix stuff," "updates," "WIP." After enabling AI commit messages:

  • Consistency: 95% of commits now follow conventional format.
  • Changelog generation: From 4 hours to 10 minutes.
  • Code archaeology: Finding when a bug was introduced: from 30 min to 2 min.

Documentation Automation

  1. Code documentation: The Avatar reads your functions and generates docstrings, type hints, and README examples.
  2. API docs: From your OpenAPI spec, it generates markdown docs with request/response examples.
  3. Architecture Decision Records (ADRs): Describe a decision in bullet points. The Avatar formats it into a standard ADR template.
  4. Onboarding docs: The Avatar interviews you about setup steps, then writes a step-by-step guide for new developers.

Framework: The Documentation Triangle

Every project needs 3 types of docs:

  • Reference: API docs, function signatures. Auto-generated, always current.
  • Tutorial: Step-by-step guides for common tasks. Written by humans, reviewed by Avatar.
  • Explanation: Why things work the way they do. Architecture, trade-offs, philosophy.

If any corner is missing, your team will struggle.

segments.title: Security Best Practices
segments.content:
Building Secure Software with AI

Security is not a feature; it is a foundation. Your Avatar helps you identify vulnerabilities, follow best practices, and maintain compliance.

Step-by-Step: Security Review Workflow

  1. Upload your security policy to PKM. Example: "OWASP Top 10 checklist," "SOC 2 requirements," or "GDPR data handling rules."
  2. Create a Security Agent in Agent Studio.
    • Prompt: "Review the provided code against the OWASP Top 10. Flag any vulnerabilities with severity (Critical, High, Medium, Low) and remediation steps."
  3. Run the agent on every pull request before human review.
  4. Review the security report. Critical and High issues must be resolved before merge.
  5. For dependencies, enable automated vulnerability scanning. The Avatar checks your package.json, requirements.txt, or Cargo.toml against known CVE databases.
  6. Schedule a monthly security audit. The Avatar reviews access logs, secret rotation status, and compliance gaps.

Case Study: The Breach That Never Happened

FinApp, a payment processing startup, ran a Security Agent on every PR. One Friday afternoon:

  • Developer pushed code with a hardcoded API key.
  • Security Agent flagged: Critical – "Hardcoded secret in config.py line 12."
  • PR blocked. Developer used environment variables instead.

Two weeks later, a security researcher scanned public repos for hardcoded keys. FinApp's competitors were breached. FinApp was safe.

Common Vulnerabilities the Avatar Detects

  • Injection attacks: SQL, NoSQL, OS command, and LDAP injection.
  • Broken authentication: Weak password policies, missing MFA, session fixation.
  • Sensitive data exposure: Unencrypted PII, hardcoded secrets, verbose error messages.
  • XXE and SSRF: XML external entities and server-side request forgery.
  • Insecure deserialization: Untrusted data passed to unserialize() or pickle.loads().

Framework: The Security Maturity Model

Rate your team on these levels:

  • Level 1 – Reactive: Fix vulnerabilities after they're found.
  • Level 2 – Defined: Security checklist for every PR. Security Agent enabled.
  • Level 3 – Proactive: Monthly audits, dependency scanning, penetration testing.
  • Level 4 – Optimised: Security is part of design. Threat modelling for every feature.

Pro Tip: Keep a "security runbook" in your PKM. When the Avatar flags an issue, the runbook tells your team exactly how to respond.

segments.title: 30-Day Coding Challenge
segments.content:
Level Up Your Development Skills

This challenge takes you from AI-assisted coding to AI-native development. Build real projects, adopt best practices, and ship faster.

Week 1: Pair Programming Foundations

  1. Day 1: Install the Zetrix IDE extension and index your current project.
  2. Day 2: Complete 5 tasks using only AI generation. Review each output for correctness.
  3. Day 3: Practice the CODE prompt framework. Write 10 prompts for real tasks.
  4. Day 4: Debug a real bug using AI. Document the root cause and fix.
  5. Day 5: Generate unit tests for a module with low coverage. Aim for 80%+.
  6. Day 6: Refactor a messy function. Ask the Avatar for 3 alternative implementations.
  7. Day 7: Review the week's AI-generated code. What patterns worked? What failed?

Week 2: Automation & Integration

  1. Day 8–10: Set up automated code review for your repository.
  2. Day 11–12: Build a small API using AI-generated scaffolding. Add auth and tests.
  3. Day 13–14: Create a no-code dashboard for a non-technical stakeholder.

Week 3: Security & Quality

  1. Day 15–17: Run a security audit on your project. Fix all Critical and High issues.
  2. Day 18–19: Automate documentation generation. Ensure every function has a docstring.
  3. Day 20–21: Set up CI/CD with AI-generated pipeline configs (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI).

Week 4: Mastery & Teaching

  1. Day 22–24: Build a complete feature end-to-end: spec → code → tests → docs → deploy.
  2. Day 25–27: Mentor a junior developer using AI-generated explanations and exercises.
  3. Day 28–29: Contribute to an open-source project. Use AI to understand the codebase and draft your PR.
  4. Day 30: Write a blog post: "How AI Changed My Development Workflow." Share your metrics: bugs caught, time saved, tests written.

Success Metrics

  • Test coverage: Target 80%+ on your main project.
  • Code review time: Reduced by 50%.
  • Documentation: 100% of public functions documented.
  • Security issues: Zero Critical/High issues remaining.
  • Features shipped: At least 1 complete end-to-end feature.

Final Thought: The best developers in the AI era are not those who write the most code. They are those who ask the best questions, review with rigour, and architect with vision.
